title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Criminals used AI-generated video and images to impersonate a real immigration attorney on social media, creating hundreds of fake profiles offering fraudulent legal services to immigrants. The scam operated across multiple platforms including TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram, with victims directed to WhatsApp contacts where fake contracts were exchanged and payment was requested through money transfer apps. This represents a deployment failure: generative AI systems created deepfakes without identity verification, and social media platforms hosted the impersonation accounts without catching them despite scale.

The failure point was not in the technology itself but in the absence of human verification at deployment. Social media platforms' automated systems did not prevent account creation using another person's likeness, and there was no gate requiring proof of identity before video or image generation could proceed. An attorney discovered the scheme only because clients called his office; without that accidental alert, the fraud would have continued undetected.

What is not established: whether the AI systems used were commercial products or custom tools, or what specific platforms' policies the scammers violated in their setup phase.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos using his likeness to promote fraudulent immigration services, including false promises of US residency for $2,200. Leal discovered the scheme last October when potential clients began calling his office, but the situation has dramatically escalated in recent months.

To combat the fraud, Leal hired an anti-piracy company that has removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts across multiple platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The scammers typically direct victims through social media videos to contact numbers on WhatsApp, where they exchange phony contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams and advises immigrants to verify anyone offering legal services online and avoid suspicious payment requests.
